Second-order control strategies, including Proportional-Integral-Derivative-Acceleration (PIDA) controllers, offer enhanced dynamic responsiveness but introduce more demanding temporal constraints. Current scheduling algorithms inadequately address these constraints, as they fail to prioritize control-critical tasks based on real-time error dynamics, resulting in suboptimal resource allocation during physiological transitions. This paper introduces Dynamic Error-Driven Rate-Harmonic Derivative-Priority (RHDP) Scheduling, a specialized RTOS scheduling algorithm designed specifically for second-order medical control systems. RHDP dynamically modifies task priorities based on both first derivatives (rate of change) and second derivatives (acceleration) of system error, ensuring optimal computational resource allocation during critical physiological transitions while maintaining the established schedulability properties of rate-monotonic scheduling. The algorithm incorporates three key innovations: Dual-Derivative Priority Adjustment: Dynamic priority modification utilizing weighted contributions from both first and second derivatives of error signals, enabling rapid response during critical system transitions. Enhanced Schedulability Analysis: Implementation of augmented Liu & Layland utilization bounds with integrated safety margins specifically calibrated for medical applications. Progressive Safety Protocol Activation: Comprehensive deadline violation monitoring with escalating safety responses triggered after multiple consecutive missed deadlines. Simulations demonstrate that RHDP considerably outperforms conventional scheduling approaches during rapid physiological changes, reducing critical response times by approximately 47% while maintaining deterministic behavior essential for medical device certification. These characteristics make RHDP particularly suitable for precision medical applications including advanced drug delivery systems for chemotherapy, hor-Abstract-Real-time scheduling algorithms for medical control systems often fail to account for the dynamic nature of physiological parameters, particularly when second-order differential controllers are employed. This paper introduces the Enhanced Rate-Harmonic Derivative-Priority (RHDP) scheduling algorithm, a novel approach that extends traditional ratemonotonic scheduling to incorporate sensitivity to both first and second derivatives of controlled variables. RHDP dynamically adjusts task priorities based on the rate of change and curvature of physiological parameters, enabling faster response to critical state changes while maintaining schedulability guarantees. We provide theoretical analysis proving RHDP's correctness and bounded response times, along with comprehensive simulations comparing it against classical scheduling techniques. Our evaluation using a disease dosage management system case study demonstrates that RHDP reduces response time by up to 47% during rapid physiological changes and improves control performance metrics including overshoot and settling time. div.head: I. INTRODUCTION
div.p: Real-time scheduling presents significant c hallenges in safety-critical medical applications, particularly in systems requiring precise dosage management and timely drug delivery control. While established scheduling algorithms such as Rate-Monotonic Scheduling (RMS) and Earliest Deadline First (EDF) have proven effective in various real-time applications, they exhibit considerable limitations when applied to medical control systems characterized by second-order dynamics. First-order PID control systems dominate current medical control applications, including insulin regulation for Type 1 Diabetes management. However, these controllers demonstrate inadequate responsiveness to rapid physiological variations, such as postprandial glucose fluctuations or exercise-induced

div.head: II. LITERATURE SURVEY
div.p: The foundations of real-time scheduling were laid by Liu and Layland, who introduced the Rate Monotonic Scheduling (RMS) and Earliest Deadline First (EDF) algorithms [1]. Their work formally established feasibility conditions for periodic tasks in hard real-time systems, setting the stage for decades of research in scheduling theory. As systems grew more complex, the concept of mixed-criticality scheduling gained prominence. Burns and Davis reviewed the state of mixed-criticality systems, identifying key challenges in task isolation, assurance levels, and graceful degradation under overload scenarios [2]. Their review remains an important reference for balancing safety-critical and non-critical workloads. In parallel, research into biomedical applications began demonstrating the potential of automated control. Steil et al. investigated the feasibility of automating insulin delivery for patients with type 1 diabetes [3]], highlighting the practical challenges in achieving closed-loop glucose regulation. Control methodologies also evolved with the introduction of eventdriven strategies. Arzén proposed a simple event-based PID controller, showing improved efficiency in situations where resources are constrained [4]. Building upon this, Cervin et al. analyzed how control performance is influenced by timing variability such as jitter, introducing simulation tools like Jitterbug and TrueTime to study the effects [5]. In the medical domain, Hovorka et al. presented a nonlinear model predictive control (MPC) approach for glucose regulation in type 1 diabetes patients, demonstrating its potential to adaptively manage blood glucose levels [6]. At the same time, broader surveys of networked control systems (NCSs), such as the work of Hespanha et al., identified communication delays, data losses, and sampling issues as central challenges in distributed control [7]. Decentralized approaches were proposed to address such issues. Wang et al. introduced DEU-CON, a decentralized end-to-end utilization control framework that enables resource-aware scheduling in distributed real-time systems [8]. Similarly, Martí et al. developed optimal state-feedback-based methods for resource allocation, ensuring efficient task execution under limited computational capacity [9]. New control paradigms also emerged, such as PIDA control. Chen, Seborg, and Braatz introduced Proportional-Integral-Derivative-Acceleration (PIDA) control strategies for multi-input multi-output (MIMO) processes with long time delays [10]. Their results highlighted improvements in stability and tracking compared to conventional PID. Energy efficiency became another major focus. Bambagini et al. surveyed strategies for energy-aware scheduling in embedded real-time systems, combining low-power techniques with timing guarantees [11]. Returning to biomedical applications, Dutta and Dutta proposed a temporal-logic-based real-time scheduling framework for automated insulin delivery systems, ensuring both correctness and timeliness of insulin administration [12]. Complementing this, Wei et al. reviewed the application of MPC in medical drug delivery, identifying key challenges and design considerations in clinical applications [13]. Research into scheduling scalability was furthered by Zhang, Burns, and Baruah, who conducted a sensitivity analysis of global fixed-priority schedulability in multiprocessor real-time systems [14]. Their work explored robustness against parameter variations, critical for large-scale deployments. In the area of IoT security, Pusuluri and Bugatha introduced TINYLOCK, a lightweight encryption algorithm designed for ATtiny85 microcontrollers. Their solution demonstrated adaptability and energy efficiency for secure IoT communications [15]. Finally, Ponnapalli and Babu emphasized the role of open-source tools in engineering research, showcasing the use of Scilab in antenna array design. Their work demonstrated the potential of open platforms for cost-effective prototyping in IoT and mechatronics [16].

div.head: IV. RHDP ALGORITHM IMPLEMENTATION
div.p: The Dynamic Error-Driven Rate-Harmonic Derivative-Priority (RHDP) scheduling algorithm comprises two primary components: the main scheduling loop and the error derivative calculation mechanism. These components work in concert to ensure optimal task prioritization based on system error dynamics.

div.head: B. Error Derivative Calculation
div.p: The RHDP algorithm maintains O(n) complexity in the number of tasks, ensuring minimal computational overhead even in resource-constrained embedded systems typically employed in portable medical devices. The dynamic priority adjustment mechanism responds immediately to error dynamics changes without requiring system reconfiguration, providing seamless adaptation to physiological variations.

div.head: A. Task Response Time Characterization
div.p: The response time characteristics of three critical tasks (Sensor Data Acquisition, Control Computation, and Safety Monitoring) under RHDP scheduling demonstrate significant improvements over traditional scheduling approaches. Figure 2 illustrates these response times across multiple operational cycles, with a deadline threshold of 2.0 ms indicated by the horizontal dashed line. During normal operation (0-40 ms), all tasks maintain response times comfortably below their deadlines. During a simulated physiological disturbance event (50-60 ms range), the Control Computation task experiences increased computational demands. Under traditional scheduling, this would result in deadline violations; however, with RHDP's dynamic priority adjustments, the response time remains constrained below critical thresholds throughout the disturbance event. Once the system returns to steady-state operation (beyond 70 ms), response times return to their nominal values. This response time management capability demonstrates RHDP's effectiveness at maintaining temporal guarantees even during significant disturbance events-a critical requirement for medical control applications where timing violations could compromise therapeutic efficacy.

div.head: B. Dynamic Priority Management Analysis
div.p: Figure 3 illustrates the dynamic priority management mechanism of RHDP, demonstrating how task priorities evolve in response to changing error dynamics. The left vertical axis represents task priority levels, while the right vertical axis displays the magnitude of error derivatives. During normal operation, priorities remain at their base RMS-assigned levels. When significant first and second derivatives are detected around the 50 ms mark (indicating rapid physiological changes), the Control Computation task priority is dynamically elevated from level 3 to level 1, ensuring it receives necessary computational resources during this critical period. As error derivatives return to normal values, priorities gradually revert to their base levels, demonstrating the algorithm's ability to temporarily reprioritize tasks during critical periods without disrupting long-term scheduling behavior.

div.head: C. Schedulability Analysis
div.p: Figure 4 presents the theoretical performance limits using the modified Liu Layland bound with the 10% safety margin implemented by RHDP. The analysis demonstrates that RHDP maintains schedulability for typical medical control applications with 5-6 concurrent tasks, with utilization remaining below the conservative bound throughout normal operation. This provides high confidence in the system's ability to meet real-time constraints under varying load conditions and physiological states.

div.head: VII. SUMMARY OF FINDINGS AND FUTURE WORKS
div.p: The comprehensive analysis of Enhanced Rate-Harmonic Derivative-Priority (RHDP) scheduling for safety-critical medical control systems reveals significant performance improvements over traditional approaches. RHDP demonstrates remarkable advantages in managing second-order control systems by incorporating both first and second derivatives of system error into its priority decision-making process. This dynamic priority adjustment mechanism enables RHDP to reduce response time by up to 50% during rapid physiological changes compared to standard rate-monotonic scheduling, which is essential for applications like precision drug delivery Tightly couples control system performance with scheduling decisions Control and scheduling typically operate independently and glucose regulation. The algorithm maintains consistent response times even during disturbance events, with critical tasks remaining below deadline thresholds due to the derivativeaware priority adjustments. RHDP's innovative approach includes explicit deadline miss detection with safety protocol triggers that provide an additional layer of protection for patient safety, activating when multiple consecutive deadlines are missed. By applying a conservative 10% safety margin to the Liu Layland utilization bound, RHDP ensures robust operation even under varying physiological and computational load conditions, addressing the stringent reliability requirements for medical device certification while maintaining deterministic behavior essential for predictable therapy delivery. The tight coupling between control system performance and scheduling decisions enables RHDP to achieve an optimal balance between real-time schedulability and physiological adaptation, making it particularly valuable for applications requiring precise control during rapid physiological changes.

div.head: VIII. FUTURE WORKS
div.p: Future research directions should focus on hardware implementation and validation of RHDP in actual medical devices, particularly exploring the performance in resource-constrained embedded systems typical of wearable and implantable med-ical technology. Additional work is needed to develop formal verification methodologies for RHDP's timing and safety guarantees that will satisfy regulatory frameworks like FDA requirements for Class III medical devices. Researchers should investigate adaptive parameter tuning mechanisms that could automatically optimize the weighting factors for derivative and acceleration components based on patient-specific physiological responses, potentially incorporating predictive models to preemptively adjust for expected changes in patient state. Furthermore, efforts should be directed toward extending RHDP to distributed medical control systems where multiple interconnected devices must coordinate treatment delivery, such as closed-loop systems combining continuous glucose monitoring with insulin delivery. Enhancement of the algorithm's monitoring capabilities could further optimize realtime performance for applications requiring dynamic physiological adaptation. Finally, comprehensive clinical studies will be necessary to quantify the therapeutic benefits of RHDP's improved response times and stability in patient outcomes, particularly for conditions requiring precise timing of drug delivery like diabetes management, Parkinson's treatment, and chemotherapy administration.

div.head: IX. CONCLUSION
div.p: Enhanced Rate-Harmonic Derivative-Priority (RHDP) Scheduling represents a significant advancement in real-time operating system scheduling for medical control applications. By integrating both first and second derivatives of system error into the priority decision-making process, RHDP provides a scheduling framework specifically optimized for second-order medical control systems. The algorithm achieves an optimal balance between real-time schedulability and physiological adaptation, making it particularly valuable for applications requiring precise control during rapid physiological changes, such as insulin delivery systems for Type 1 Diabetes and precision drug delivery systems for chemotherapy and hormone therapy. RHDP's ability to detect and respond to both the rate of change and acceleration in physiological parameters provides a substantial improvement over conventional scheduling techniques. Its dynamic priority adjustment mechanism ensures control tasks receive appropriate execution time precisely when needed, while the conservative schedulability analysis with safety margins ensures the robustness essential for medical applications. As medical devices continue to evolve toward higher precision and autonomy, scheduling algorithms like RHDP that specifically address the unique requirements of second-order control systems will play an increasingly important role in ensuring safe and effective therapy delivery. This innovation bridges the gap between theoretical algorithmic advancements and practical implementation in patient-centric therapeutic solutions.
